title: Air France 4590 (Concorde)

agencies.name: Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses pour la sécurité de l'aviation civile
agencies.report_title: Accident on 25 July 2000 at La Patte d'Oie in Gonesse (95) to the Concorde registered F-BTSC operated by Air France

location.name: Hotel at La Patte d'Oie, Gonesse, 9.5 km from Paris CDG

summary: During the takeoff roll on runway 26R at Charles de Gaulle, Concorde F-BTSC ran over a titanium alloy strip that had fallen from a Continental Airlines DC-10 minutes earlier. The strip cut the right front tyre of the left main gear, which burst; a large piece of tyre struck the underside of the wing, causing a shock wave that ruptured fuel tank 5. Leaking fuel ignited, engines 1 and 2 lost thrust, the gear could not be retracted, and the aircraft, unable to climb or accelerate, lost control and crashed onto a hotel in Gonesse. All 109 on board and 4 on the ground died.
probable_cause: The accident was due to: the high-speed passage of a tyre over a part lost by an aircraft that had taken off five minutes earlier and the destruction of the tyre; the ripping out of a large piece of tank 5 from the underside of the wing through a complex process of transmission of the energy from the tyre debris; ignition of the leaking fuel by an electric arc in the landing gear bay or by contact with hot parts of the engine, and the propagation of the fire; the impossibility of retracting the landing gear, which probably contributed to the loss of thrust on engine 1 and the loss of control. Contributing: the strip had been installed on the DC-10 in a non-conforming manner, and previous tyre-burst incidents on Concorde had not led to protective measures against tank rupture.

factors.evidence: The titanium wear strip on the Continental DC-10 thrust reverser cowl had been manufactured and fitted in a non-conforming manner and detached on takeoff, leaving it on runway 26R.
Concorde had suffered numerous tyre bursts and several tank penetrations since 1979 without measures adequate to prevent fuel tank rupture.
The wing fuel tanks were vulnerable to rupture from tyre debris impacts and the tyres were prone to catastrophic destruction on foreign object damage.
Certification did not address the risk of tank rupture from tyre debris at the energy levels shown to be possible.
Tank 5 was ruptured from within by a pressure wave and fuel escaped at a very high rate under the left wing.
The fuel ignited, producing a very large flame trailing from the left wing and damaging the airframe and controls.
Engine 2 surged and lost thrust and was shut down; engine 1 also lost thrust twice, the second time irrecoverably.
The landing gear could not be retracted, probably because of fire damage to gear bay wiring, preventing acceleration and climb.
With two engines lost, the gear down and the aircraft below V2, it could neither accelerate nor climb above about 200 ft.
The aircraft pitched up and rolled left beyond 100 degrees, and struck the ground at low speed and high angle of attack.
The aircraft was destroyed by impact and fire on striking a hotel in Gonesse, killing four people on the ground.

events.text: A Continental Airlines DC-10 takes off from runway 26R; a 43 cm titanium wear strip from its number 3 engine thrust reverser cowl falls onto the runway.
Concorde begins its takeoff roll on runway 26R, about a tonne over the maximum takeoff weight with a light tailwind.
At about 175 kt, after V1, the number 2 tyre on the left main gear runs over the metal strip and bursts; tyre debris strikes the wing and tank 5 ruptures.
Leaking fuel ignites; a large flame trails from under the left wing. Engines 1 and 2 surge and lose thrust.
Tower controller informs the crew that they have strong flames behind them.
Engine 2 fire alarm sounds; the captain rotates and the aircraft lifts off at about 205 kt with engine 1 recovering thrust.
Flight engineer shuts down engine 2 and pulls the fire handle; the crew call for gear retraction.
The landing gear does not retract despite the selection; the aircraft climbs slowly to about 200 ft at about 200 kt.
Crew declare an emergency and attempt to reach Le Bourget; the aircraft cannot accelerate or climb.
Engine 1 loses thrust a second time; with only engines 3 and 4 on the right the aircraft pitches up and rolls steeply left.
Aircraft strikes the Hotelissimo hotel at La Patte d'Oie, Gonesse, in a nose-high left-banked attitude; all 109 occupants and 4 people on the ground killed.

recommendations.text: Suspend the Concorde certificate of airworthiness until measures are taken to guarantee a satisfactory level of safety with respect to tyre destruction and its consequences on the fuel tanks.
recommendations.outcome: Certificates suspended in August 2000; Kevlar tank liners, new Michelin NZG tyres and armoured wiring were introduced before return to service in November 2001.

recommendations.text: Strengthen the requirements and inspection of runways for foreign object debris, and ensure that repairs on aircraft parts liable to fall on runways conform to approved data.
Study tyre-destruction models and the effects of tyre debris on aircraft structures and fuel tanks for certification of large aircraft.

safety_changes: Kevlar-rubber liners in Concorde fuel tanks, Michelin NZG near-zero-growth tyres, armoured gear bay wiring; return to service in November 2001.
Increased runway FOD inspection frequency at Paris airports and broader FOD awareness programmes.
Concorde withdrawn from service by both operators in 2003.

notes: Continental Airlines and its mechanics were prosecuted and Continental disputed the findings in court, but no accredited agency formally dissented; dissent is empty.
Clock times are UTC as used in the BEA report; intermediate event seconds are approximate (tyre burst about 14:43:13, impact about 14:44:31).
Occupants counts the 109 on board; fatalities of 113 include 4 persons on the ground.
Some speeds (175 kt at tyre burst, lift-off about 205 kt) are approximate values from the report.
